newsitem.title: USA: Gun in Martin Luther King case to be re-tested.
newsitem.headline: Gun in Martin Luther King case to be re-tested.

text.p: Ballistic tests were to be conducted on Wednesday at a University of Rhode Island crime lab on the rifle that may have been used to kill Martin Luther King Jr.
The Remington rifle and the bullet pulled from civil rights leader King's body were brought to the laboratory for scientists to test for the third time.
The new ballistic tests could win a retrial for James Earl Ray, who pleaded guilty to the 1968 King assassination at a Memphis, Tennessee, hotel but then recanted his story.
Ray's fingerprints were found on the weapon, but it was never proven to be the murder weapon. Prior testing in 1968 and 1978 were inconclusive.

"There very well could be a better chance of observing this under the new technology," URI criminologist Robert Hathaway told reporters. "And here again, it's just an option. Let's take science one step further and see if yes or no, there is something that can be done."

Hathaway and two other scientists, Marshall Robinson from the Connecticut State Police laboratory and George Reich from the Suffolk County police laboratory on Long Island, New York, will fire the weapon 18 times into a 900-gallon water tank.
Then they will compare the test bullets with the one that killed King under several high-powered microscopes. The results will be sent to a Pennsylvania laboratory next week for further study.
Under Tennessee law a closed case may be re-opened if there is a reasonable possibility that technology, not available at the time of the crime, could prove a person's innocence.
But it is uncertain whether Ray will every get his day in court. The 69-year-old drifter and small-time crook is seriously ill with liver disease.
